title: Squashed Hashtag
story: A screen reader reads posts aloud for people who cannot see the screen. Hashtags are a problem: #lemoncakerecipe is one long run of letters, and reading it letter by letter is useless. The reader has a list of known words and tries to cut each hashtag into them, so it can say "lemon cake recipe".
Before trying to say anything, it needs to know whether a clean cut exists at all.
task: Write canSplit(tag, words). Return true if tag can be cut into pieces so that every piece is in words, and false otherwise.
Every letter must belong to exactly one piece, and pieces keep their order. A word can be used any number of times. The tag has no # and is all lowercase.
constraints: tag and words contain only lowercase letters a to z.

examples.explanation: Cut it as lemon | cake | recipe. (lemon | cake | rec | ipe also works; one clean cut is enough.)
start | up | week works. Grabbing the shortest word first takes "star" and leaves "tupweek", which nothing fits. So you must be ready to try a different first word.
night | owl leaves a lone "s". nigh leaves "towls", and "towel" does not match it. No cut covers every letter.

hints: In startupweek, suppose you already know that the first 7 letters, startup, can be cut cleanly. What is the only thing left to check for the whole tag?
The rest, week, must be one word. More generally: the first i letters can be cut if, for some earlier point j, the first j letters can be cut and the letters from j to i form one word.
Keep a list ok where ok[i] says whether the first i letters can be cut. ok[0] is true: the empty start needs no words. Fill it from left to right.
For each i, try only the last-word lengths from 1 to 20 (no word is longer). If ok[i - len] is true and tag.slice(i - len, i) is in a set of the words, mark ok[i] true. The answer is ok[tag.length].
bruteForce: Try every word that matches the start of the tag, then recursively do the same on what is left. Backtrack when you get stuck.

On a tag like forty as followed by a b, with words a, aa, aaa, every split of the as is tried before the recursion learns that the b can never be covered. That is billions of splits. The recursion keeps asking "can the rest from position 20 be cut?" again and again, and the answer never changes.

js: * @param {string[]} words  known words, each usable many times
* @return {boolean} true if the tag can be cut entirely into known words
py: def can_split(tag: str, words: list[str]) -> bool:

js: for (const w of words) longest = Math.max(longest, w.length);
// ok[i] = can the first i letters be cut into known words?
for (let len = 1; len <= longest && len <= i && !ok[i]; len++) {
// the last word is tag[i - len .. i)
if (ok[i - len] && known.has(tag.slice(i - len, i))) ok[i] = true;
py: longest = max(len(w) for w in words)
# ok[i] = can the first i letters be cut into known words?
for length in range(1, min(longest, i) + 1):
# the last word is tag[i - length : i]
if ok[i - length] and tag[i - length:i] in known:
walkthrough: Whatever the cut, it has a last word. If the last word covers letters j to i, then the first j letters must be cuttable on their own. So ok[i] is true when some ok[j] is true and tag[j..i) is a word.
Trace startupweek with words star, start, up, week. Positions are letter counts:
• ok[4]: "star" is a word and ok[0] is true, so true.
• ok[5]: "start" is a word and ok[0] is true, so true.
• ok[6]: the true spots so far are 0, 4 and 5, so the last word would be "startu", "tu" or "u". None are words. False.
• ok[7]: "up" follows ok[5], true. (From ok[4] the rest would be "tup", not a word.)
Unlike the greedy tries, the table keeps every reachable cut point at once, so a dead end after "star" costs nothing: "start" is already recorded.
solution.timeWhy: For each of the n positions, up to L word lengths, and each slice and hash costs up to L (L ≤ 20).
solution.spaceWhy: The ok table plus the word set.
solution.takeaway: For "can this string be built from pieces" questions, mark which prefix lengths are reachable. Each position looks back by every possible piece length. It is the same shape as packing an exact order from fixed box sizes, with words in place of boxes.
